title: Harvest home
hook: harvest festivals and Thanksgiving mark the end of the year's work

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukkot: a roof of branches, more shade than sun, and room for the stranger. Your line was the booth. Have you found your meal outside yet? Today, the moment the last load comes in. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

Harvest home. In English country tradition, those two words named a moment: the last wagon of sheaves coming up the lane toward the barn, and the field finally bare. Tradition says a supper followed, for everyone who had worked the field, the farmer and the laborers at one table. The words made their way into hymns. In the United States and Canada, a Thanksgiving table can still carry some of that feeling: a season's work done, and a meal to mark it. Today: harvest home.
screen: `THE LAST LOAD COMES IN.` → `ONE TABLE FOR EVERYONE.` → `HARVEST HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the song. An English hymn by Henry Alford puts today's word in its second line: "Come, ye thankful people, come, Raise the song of harvest home: All is safely gathered in, Ere the winter storms begin." Notice what it celebrates. Not the profit. The relief. The work is done, and done in time. Second, the tears behind it. A psalm puts the harvest in a longer story. In the King James words: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." The sowing was hard. Some of it happened in bad years and worried seasons. The joy at harvest is the same field, seen from the other end. Third, the full table. Deuteronomy pictures a people settled in a good land and eating their fill, and says, in the King James words: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee." The next verses warn why: a full house is where forgetting starts. So the thanks is set at the moment of plenty, not only in the lean years. Jewish tradition takes this verse as the root of the blessing said after meals. Fourth, your own field. You may never bring in wheat. But a year of work has a harvest too: a project finished, a child grown a little, a skill that wasn't there before, a hard season gotten through. And some of it may have been sown in tears. A harvest festival is a pause to look at what's gathered, call it by name, and give thanks, before the next season starts.
screen: `ALL IS SAFELY GATHERED IN.` · `SOW IN TEARS, REAP IN JOY.` · `BLESS WHEN YOU ARE FULL.` · `YOUR OWN FIELD.` · then, large: `HARVEST HOME.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Look back over this year of your work, paid or unpaid. Let three things you've gathered come to mind, one at a time. Something finished. Something learned. Something survived. Name each one, quietly. If one of them was sown in tears, let that be part of it. Then think of one person who helped you bring it in, and let their face come to mind. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words. If not, just say thank you, to whoever comes to mind. The bell holds the time.
Harvest home. The old name for the moment the last load is in, with a supper and thanks for the year's work. Today's word.
Your line: harvest home. Today, tell one person something you gathered this year, and thank someone who helped you bring it in. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: At harvest festivals, churches and communities decorate with produce, sing harvest hymns and share a meal, and the gifts are sometimes given away; Thanksgiving brings families together around a shared table.
